definition: What it costs to pay off a track ahead of schedule. It is not uniform. Prime and variable tracks carry no capitalisation-difference fee, because the bank takes no interest-rate risk on them. Fixed tracks do. And on a CPI-linked track there is an "average index" component that applies only if you repay between the 1st and the 15th of the month — repay from the 16th to month-end and it does not apply at all.
A third party (usually a family member or friend with a salary) who signs the lease. If the tenant stops paying rent, the landlord can collect from the Arev.

A guarantor, or guarantors. These are people (landlords commonly ask for two , usually Israeli residents) who sign a promissory note and pay your debt if you default. A signature, not cash, so it sits outside the legal deposit cap. Who can sign, what they risk, and how to push back: guarantors (arevim) for a rental .
municipal property tax, paid by whoever occupies the property.

A bank guarantee: your bank promises to pay the landlord on demand and freezes that full amount of your own money for the lease term. Since a February 2025 reform, the fee on a deposit-backed residential guarantee up to NIS 50,000 is a flat sum of roughly NIS 250 to 410. How it works, the frozen-cash cost, and when to refuse one: the bank guarantee, explained .

When buying “on paper” (pre-construction), your money should go to a special project account managed by a bank, not directly to the developer. This guarantees your money is safe if the developer goes bankrupt.
for the policy rate, inflation, and mortgage rules.
the engineer inspection of a property before you buy.
the Central Bureau of Statistics, for prices, starts, and inventory.
a housing company that holds registration for some older buildings before title moves into Tabu.
the rental contract itself, the document everything above is named inside.

Tofes 4 (Occupancy Permit) The “Form 4” is the finish line. It is the official certificate from the municipality that a new building is safe, connected to utilities (water/power), and fit for habitation. Never move into a new building without Tofes 4.
A water tank connected to solar panels on the roof. It provides free hot water during the summer. Most apartments have them (except for very tall towers).
the national map for zoning and planning. See how to use these on evaluating a deal .
Every property in Israel has an ID number used for identification.
the block, parcel, and sub-parcel numbers that identify a property.

Index-linkage: the lease clause that lets your rent rise with the official price index. It is the verb form of the madad (below); if your contract has this line, your rent is not actually fixed. How to read the clause and do the maths: index-linked rent and the madad .
betterment levy, normally 50% of the value uplift from a planning change. See taxes .
The license to build or renovate. You cannot legally close a balcony, build a pergola, or add a room without a Heter.
a warning note registered on title that protects a buyer between signing and full registration.
the state body that leases most land. About 93% of Israel is state land leased for 49 or 99 years; only about 7% is private freehold.
A document from the bank confirming they agree in principle to lend you X amount of money. Always get this before signing a contract.
The company building the project. When buying new, check the Kablan’s classification (Sivug) to ensure they are financially stable and experienced.

These two sound almost identical and behave very differently. קל"צ is fixed and not linked — the balance is a fixed number of shekels and the payment never moves. ק"צ is fixed but CPI-linked — the interest rate is fixed, but the balance grows with inflation, so the shekel payment rises. And there is a regulatory consequence: for the Bank of Israel's track-mix rule, only קל"צ counts as the protected fixed third. ק"צ is counted in the variable bucket.

Israelis value airflow. Properties are described by how many “directions” they have (North, South, East, West). An apartment with “3 directions” allows for cross-breeze and is worth more than one with “1 direction.”
the share a bank will lend. Caps are 75% for a first home, 70% for a replacement home, and 50% for an investor or additional property.

A private storage unit, usually a small locked room in the basement, the parking level, or beside the flat. Worth confirming it is actually included and not billed as an extra. What to check when a listing promises one: the apartment viewing checklist .
the occupier, the legal word that makes the tenant (not the owner) liable for arnona.
the consumer price index that CPI-linked loans and some contracts track.
the reinforced safe room required in newer apartments.
The bank's markup over the anchor rate. This is the part that is negotiable, and where a broker earns their fee.
purchase tax, paid by the buyer. Most foreign and investor buyers pay 8% up to 6,055,070 NIS and 10% above. See Israel real estate taxes .
capital gains tax, 25% on the real (inflation-adjusted) gain.
a mortgage. See financing and mortgages .
VAT, 18% since January 2025, charged on new-build developer sales. See VAT on Israeli property .
An open-air balcony (not enclosed with glass). In Israel, a large balcony is a major value driver.

A shared or public bomb shelter, often in the basement or down the street, the fallback for older buildings that have no in-flat safe room. In the Home Front Command order of protection it ranks below a mamad and a shared-floor room. How to score a building that relies on one: the safe room and shelter check .

About 90% of land in Israel is state-owned. If a property is “Minhal” (or Rameen ), you are technically acquiring a long-term lease (usually 49 or 99 years) rather than private ownership. This is very common and secure, but the bureaucratic process differs from Tabu.

A balcony or veranda. Common, pleasant, and occasionally counted into the floor area that drives your arnona, so check what you are paying for. Covered alongside the rest of the flat’s features at the apartment viewing checklist .

Mas Rechisha (Purchase Tax) A tiered government tax paid by the buyer. Rates vary based on residency status (Israeli vs. Foreigner) and whether this is your first or second home. New Immigrants (Olim) often receive a discounted tier.
The Hebrew word for a mortgage: a loan secured against a property. Israeli mashkanta is normally split into several tracks with different interest bases.

A situation where land or a building hasn’t been legally subdivided yet. Instead of owning “Apartment 4,” you own “10% of the building.” This is common in older areas but makes getting a mortgage more complex.
the Tax Authority database of recorded transaction prices.
the title extract that shows the owner, mortgages, liens, and any warning note.
The official document printed from the Tabu. It proves who owns the apartment, the exact size (in sqm), and details any mortgages or attachments to the property.
The interest-rate base a track is built on — prime, a government bond yield, or another index. The bank adds its margin on top of the anchor.
Choose what you want to allow.
A clause in a rental contract that allows the tenant to extend the lease for another year (usually at the same price or a pre-agreed minimal increase). This is crucial for stability.

Tabu (Land Registry) The Israel Land Registry office. “Tabu” is the gold standard of ownership. A “Clean Tabu” means the property is fully registered in the seller’s name, with specific sub-parcel rights (like specific parking spots), and has no hidden liens or debts.

Your security deposit, the cash-equivalent the landlord holds against unpaid rent or damage. By law it is capped at the lower of one-third of the total lease rent or three months rent (for any lease of nine months or more, three months rent is the binding figure), and it must come back within 60 days of the lease ending. The cap, the maths, and how to get it back: the rental security deposit .
evacuate and rebuild renewal, which needs two-thirds owner consent to override a refusing minority.
the bank prime rate, set at the Bank of Israel rate plus 1.5%.
A document signed on move-in day. It lists the condition of the apartment, furniture, and meter readings (water/electric). It protects you from being blamed for pre-existing damage when you leave.
The share of your net monthly income that goes to loan repayments. Capped at 50%; above 40% the bank must apply a 100% risk weight, which raises the rate.

this page defines the Hebrew and technical terms you meet when you buy, finance, or check an Israeli property, grouped by where they come up. Each term gets one plain line. Where a term has its own deep guide in this hub, the term links to it. For the full picture start at the Israel real estate investment hub .
Arev (Guarantor) A third party (usually a family member or friend with a salary) who signs the lease. If the tenant stops paying rent, the landlord can collect from the Arev.

Dampness held in walls, the ceiling, or the sand under the floor, showing as stains, peeling plaster or mould. Hiding it from a buyer is illegal in Israel, and as a renter it is the single defect most worth spotting at a viewing. How to find it: the building inspection checklist .
a licensed appraiser whose valuation the bank relies on.
a security check, usually undated, held aside against damage and not cashed unless something goes wrong.
a promissory note, the IOU your arevim sign so the landlord can collect a fixed sum on default.
the national land registry where ownership is recorded. See due diligence .
the former national plan for seismic reinforcement, now closed to new permit applications. See urban renewal .

Your mortgage is not one loan. It is a blend of tracks, and the blend is called the tamhil . When an Israeli adviser asks what tamhil you want, they are asking how you want to divide your borrowing between prime, fixed non-linked and CPI-linked. There is no single correct answer — it depends on your income currency, your time horizon, and how much payment uncertainty you can absorb.

Each term routes to one page that explains it in full. Two terms can share a home page (mamad and miklat both live on the safety page, for instance) and still get their own line and link here. Read this table as the routing slip for the whole rental section.

Mamad (Safe Room) Merchav Mugan Dirati. A reinforced concrete room mandatory in all buildings built after 1992. It protects against rocket attacks and earthquakes. It functions as a regular bedroom but has a heavy steel door and window.

The renting world hands you twelve money-and-safety words you cannot ignore: arnona, arev/arevim, arvut bankait, hatzmada la-madad, machsan, madad, mamad, mirpeset, miklat, pinui binui, tama 38, vaad bayit. The thirteenth, easy to miss because it hides under the guarantee words, is pikadon , the deposit itself, the parent idea that the bank guarantee and the guarantors are merely two ways to secure. That is twelve named terms plus pikadon, which earns its own line as the umbrella the deposit-and-guarantee family hangs from. Thirteen core entries in all, none padded in, none quietly missing.
the occupancy permit that lets you legally move into a new build.
the building committee that collects monthly fees and manages shared areas. See due diligence .
A private gas system for heating water and radiators. It provides instant hot water 24/7, essential for winters in Jerusalem or the North.
a short preliminary memo that can legally bind you. Do not sign one casually. See the buying process .
A bank's written indication of how much it will lend you and on what terms, issued after reviewing income and documents. It typically holds for a limited period.

term_latin: ביטוח חיים למשכנתא Mortgage life insurance
definition: A decreasing life policy assigned to the bank that repays the outstanding balance if the borrower dies. Effectively required by every Israeli lender.
A loan where a large part of the principal is repaid at the end rather than amortised. Common in developer "pay later" deals; the Bank of Israel caps these at 10% of a bank's quarterly approvals.
The central bank. Its Monetary Committee sets the policy rate, and its Supervisor of Banks sets the rules on loan-to-value, term and track mix.
A period at the start of the loan where you pay interest only, or nothing at all. It lowers early payments but increases the total cost.
Your own cash contribution. The Bank of Israel sets minimum equity through the maximum loan-to-value ceiling for each buyer type.
The Israeli land registry. The bank registers a mortgage charge against the property there, and the charge is removed once the loan is repaid.
The standard Israeli repayment method: equal total monthly payments, with the interest share falling and the principal share rising over the term. Mathematically an annuity.
The consumer price index published by the Central Bureau of Statistics. "Madad-linked" means the loan balance tracks this index.
Replacing an existing mashkanta with new terms, either with the same bank or a different one, usually to cut the rate or change the track mix.
The tax paid on acquiring Israeli property. The rate depends on the price, whether it is your only home, and your residency status.
A loan against home equity for older owners, repaid when the property is sold or the owner vacates, rather than monthly.
A new immigrant to Israel under the Law of Return, entitled to specific purchase-tax reliefs and other benefits, including in mortgage pricing.

term_latin: עמלת פירעון מוקדם Early repayment fee
definition: A charge for paying off a fixed or linked track ahead of schedule, calculated from the gap between your rate and current market rates. Prime-linked tracks normally carry no such fee.
Keren Tzmuda, "linked principal". A fixed interest rate, but the outstanding balance is linked to the consumer price index, so the shekel payment rises with inflation.
Keren Lo Tzmuda, literally "not linked principal". A fixed interest rate that is not linked to the consumer price index. The most predictable track: the payment is set at signing and never moves.
A repayment method where the principal is repaid in equal slices, so total payments start higher and decline. It costs less interest overall than Spitzer.
The Bank of Israel policy rate plus 1.5 percentage points. Every change in the Bank of Israel rate moves prime immediately and by the same amount.
Bank of Israel rules obliging banks to disclose the cost of a mortgage in a standard format, so offers can be compared like for like.
An independent valuation of the property, commissioned by the bank, that sets the ceiling for how much the bank will finance.
